items.stem: What is an idiolect?
options: The language of a whole country
An individual’s unique way of using language
items.answer: An individual’s unique way of using language
items.markingKey: Shaped by region, age, occupation, interests and experiences.

items.stem: A sociolinguistics textbook gives this example: “Surfers share terms such as ‘gnarly’ and ‘barrel’ that outsiders rarely use.” Identify what it illustrates and explain your answer.
items.answer: Sociolect: language shared by a social group.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies sociolect; explains with reference to the example (language shared by a social group); links to a relevant concept, theory or context.

items.stem: A student investigating language and identity records this: ‘A student uses Hindi with her grandmother and English with friends, sometimes in the same sentence.’ Identify what it illustrates and explain your answer.
items.answer: Code-switching: moving between languages or varieties according to context or for effect.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies code-switching; explains with reference to the example (moving between languages or varieties according to context or for effect); links to a relevant concept, theory or context.

items.stem: A student in Lima recorded the use of dropped /h/ (e.g. ’ouse) in interviews. Number of non-standard tokens / total tokens: middle-class men: 18/40; middle-class women: 13/60; working-class men: 52/80; working-class women: 38/80. Calculate the percentage of non-standard forms for each group (to 1 decimal place).
items.answer: middle-class men: 18 ÷ 40 × 100 = 45.0%. middle-class women: 13 ÷ 60 × 100 = 21.7%. working-class men: 52 ÷ 80 × 100 = 65.0%. working-class women: 38 ÷ 80 × 100 = 47.5%.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks: correct percentages (middle-class men 45.0%; middle-class women 21.7%; working-class men 65.0%; working-class women 47.5%).

items.stem: A student in Karachi recorded the use of dropped /h/ (e.g. ’ouse) in interviews. Number of non-standard tokens / total tokens: middle-class men: 34/80; working-class men: 46/60; working-class women: 32/60; middle-class women: 8/60. Calculate the percentage of non-standard forms for each group (to 1 decimal place) and analyse what the results suggest, with reference to research.
items.answer: middle-class men: 34 ÷ 80 × 100 = 42.5%. working-class men: 46 ÷ 60 × 100 = 76.7%. working-class women: 32 ÷ 60 × 100 = 53.3%. middle-class women: 8 ÷ 60 × 100 = 13.3%. Highest: working-class men; lowest: middle-class women. This pattern resembles Trudgill’s findings (class and gender stratification; covert prestige for men).
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks: correct percentages (middle-class men 42.5%; working-class men 76.7%; working-class women 53.3%; middle-class women 13.3%); interpretation of class/gender patterns; reference to Trudgill or Labov; awareness of small sample sizes.

items.stem: Who wrote Language and Woman’s Place (1975)?
items.answer: Robin Lakoff
items.markingKey: Lakoff proposed a list of features of ‘women’s language’.

items.answer: Deficit: Lakoff (1975) presented women’s language as lacking authority.

items.stem: A student recorded a group discussion in Madrid. The male speakers produced 1,800 words and 36 tag questions; the female speakers produced 3,200 words and 25 tag questions. Calculate the rate of tag questions per 1,000 words for each group (to 1 decimal place).
items.answer: Male: 36 ÷ 1,800 × 1,000 = 20.0. Female: 25 ÷ 3,200 × 1,000 = 7.8. Male speakers used them more often.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks: normalising by word count; male 20.0, female 7.8 per 1,000 words.

items.stem: A student recorded a group discussion in Bangkok. The male speakers produced 2,400 words and 11 minimal responses (mm, yeah); the female speakers produced 1,600 words and 17 minimal responses (mm, yeah). Calculate the rate of minimal responses (mm, yeah) per 1,000 words for each group (to 1 decimal place). Then evaluate what the results show about gender and talk, referring to research.
items.answer: Male: 11 ÷ 2,400 × 1,000 = 4.6. Female: 17 ÷ 1,600 × 1,000 = 10.6. Female speakers used them more often. Interpretation must be cautious: one small sample, functions vary (e.g. Holmes: facilitative v. epistemic tags), and context, role and power may matter more than gender (Cameron, O’Barr and Atkins).
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks: normalising by word count; male 4.6, female 10.6 per 1,000 words; evaluation referring to Lakoff/Holmes/Cameron and the limits of the data.

items.stem: Who developed communication accommodation theory?

items.stem: Read this transcript from a classroom: ‘TEACHER: right (.) phones away please (.) Omar (.) that includes you OMAR: I’m just checking the time miss TEACHER: there’s a clock (.) look up OMAR: [laughs] fair enough TEACHER: thank you’ Analyse how power and politeness are shown in the interaction, referring to relevant theories.
items.answer: Teacher’s bald-on-record directives (‘phones away’); Naming as a face-threatening act; Omar’s excuse and humour to save face; Teacher’s ‘thank you’ restores politeness; Institutional power behind discourse (school roles).

items.stem: Read this transcript from a doctor’s consultation: ‘DOCTOR: and how long have you had the pain PATIENT: about a week (.) I didn’t want to bother you DOCTOR: you’re not bothering me at all (.) let’s have a look PATIENT: thank you (.) sorry DOCTOR: no need to apologise (.) can you lie down for me’ Analyse how power and politeness are shown in the interaction, referring to relevant theories.
